c.tagline: China's thousand-year Porcelain Capital, where the kilns still glow.

taxi.fareNote: Meters start around ¥8 for the first 2 km; ride-hailing via Didi is common and cheap. Few drivers speak English, so have your destination written in Chinese.

emergency.note: 110 police, 120 ambulance, 119 fire. English is rarely spoken—keep your location written in Chinese characters.

hood_desc: The historic heart of the Porcelain Capital around the Imperial Kiln Museum, Zhushan (Pearl Hill), and the old ceramic workshops; the most convenient walkable base, with markets, street food, and porcelain shops at every turn.

A regenerated ceramics-factory complex turned buzzing cultural quarter, with galleries, design studios, cafes, craft-beer bars, and a lively weekend creative market—Jingdezhen's trendiest, most international area.

A green valley just south of town lined with independent ceramic studios, artist residencies, boutique guesthouses, and farm-to-table cafes; a tranquil, bohemian retreat popular with the young 'Jingpiao' artists who flock here.

The modern administrative and residential side of the city across the Chang River, with newer hotels, malls, and wide avenues; quieter and less touristy, suited to travelers wanting contemporary comforts.

water.note: Drink bottled or boiled water, as locals do.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 6:00 AM to 9:30 PM; after that taxis and Didi fill the gap.
transit.note: Jingdezhen has no metro or tram; a network of around 20 public bus lines plus plentiful taxis and Didi ride-hailing cover the city.
transit.pay: Buses are a flat ¥1-2 paid in cash (exact change) or by mobile QR (Alipay/WeChat); there is no tourist transit card. Taxis start at about ¥8.

bus: Intercity coaches from Jingdezhen Bus Terminal

car.idp: Not recognized — China requires a Chinese driving permit

transit.m: Airport shuttle bus to city center (~30 min)

tip.r: Tipping is not customary in China and may even be refused; there is no service charge at most restaurants.

food.name: Leng fen
food.desc: The porcelain city's signature snack: cool, springy rice jelly noodles tossed in chilli oil with pickled radish and shreds of dried orange peel.

places.name: Maozai Specialty Snacks (Shengli Road)
places.note: Named the one-stop spot for leng fen and jiaozi ba in local restaurant round-ups.

places.name: Fuzhou Nong Snack Street
places.note: Historic snack lane where several stalls have made leng fen the same way for decades.

places.name: Sanlumiao Food Street
places.note: Evening food street next to the ceramics market; cheap bowls eaten standing up.

food.name: Jiaozi ba
food.desc: Steamed rice-flour dumplings with a translucent skin, filled with minced pork, bamboo shoot and chilli; eaten for breakfast across Jingdezhen.

places.name: Fuzhou Nong Snack Street

food.name: Jian shui ba
food.desc: Alkaline rice cakes, chewy and faintly yellow, either stir-fried with chilli and greens or sliced into soup; an old Jingdezhen kiln-worker staple.

places.name: Fuzhou Nong Snack Street

places.name: Yanlao Family Kitchen

places.name: Sanlumiao Food Street

food.desc: Jiangxi rice noodles in a clear or chilli broth topped with pressed salted duck, a bowl found on almost every corner of the old town.

food.desc: Green tea from Fuliang county just north of the city, traded here since the Tang dynasty and brewed, naturally, in local porcelain cups.

places.name: Jingdezhen Night Market

landmarks: Taoxichuan Ceramic Art Avenue
A stylishly converted 1950s porcelain factory district of brick kilns and chimneys, now buzzing with galleries, studios, night markets and young ceramic artists.
Imperial Kiln Museum
An award-winning museum of sweeping brick vaults built over the Ming-Qing imperial kiln ruins, displaying exquisite shards and treasures once fired exclusively for emperors.
Ancient Kiln Folk Customs Museum (Guyao)
A living-history park where master artisans demonstrate every stage of traditional porcelain making around the world's oldest working wood-fired dragon kilns.
Jingdezhen China Ceramics Museum
A monumental modern museum tracing 2,000 years of porcelain history, from Song-dynasty shadow-blue ware to Mao-era propaganda ceramics, atop a landscaped hill.
Longzhu Pavilion (Dragon Pearl Pavilion)
A rebuilt Ming-style pavilion crowning Zhushan hill on the imperial kiln site, long the symbol of the porcelain capital and its emperor-appointed supervisors.
Sanbao Ceramic Art Village
A bohemian valley of studios, water-powered clay hammers and international residencies, where contemporary ceramists work amid bamboo groves and rustic farmhouse kilns.
Yaoli Ancient Town
The birthplace of Jingdezhen's porcelain industry, this riverside village of Huizhou-style houses, ancient kiln sites and tea terraces makes an idyllic day trip.
Hutian Ancient Kiln Site
The excavated remains of the Song and Yuan dynasties' most celebrated folk kilns, where the ethereal qingbai 'shadow-blue' glaze was perfected.
Taoyangli Historic District
The restored heart of old porcelain Jingdezhen, its alleys of kiln-brick houses, guild halls and workshops wrap around the Imperial Kiln Museum.
Fuliang Ancient County Town and Red Pagoda
A preserved county seat north of the city, featuring a Qing-dynasty yamen courthouse and the leaning 1,000-year-old Song-dynasty Red Pagoda.

train.note: Jingdezhen has no international trains. High-speed services use Jingdezhen North on the Nanchang-Jingdezhen-Huangshan line, putting Huangshan and Nanchang within a couple of hours, while the older Jingdezhen station handles conventional long-distance trains - the 2182/2183 leaves Shanghai at 12:40 and takes about 16 hours (¥117 hard sleeper) and the K645 from Beijing runs nearly 24 hours for ¥361-552 depending on the class of berth. There are three direct trains a day from Nanchang, though the bus is quicker on that leg. Book on 12306 with your passport.

bus.note: No international coaches serve Jingdezhen. Long-distance buses use the western bus station and the Licun station on Shuguang Lu; services from Hangzhou West leave at 09:00 and 14:20, cost about ¥140 and take around 7 hours, Nanchang's Qingshan Road North station is about 3 hours and ¥79, and Wuyuan is 2 hours away, making the bus the sensible link to the Huizhou villages. Tickets are bought at the terminal counters.

ferry.note: Jingdezhen stands on the Chang River, which carried the porcelain trade for centuries but no longer has any scheduled passenger boats. There are no ferry services to or from the city today.

half.name: Wuyuan Ancient Villages
half.blurb: Hui-style villages of white-walled courtyard houses in neighboring Jiangxi countryside, about an hour from Jingdezhen.

half.name: Poyang Lake
half.blurb: China's largest freshwater lake, known for migratory bird flocks in winter and fishing villages along its shore.

full.name: Mount Sanqing
full.blurb: A UNESCO-listed granite peak with sheer cliffs and pine-covered ridges, roughly three hours from Jingdezhen.
